summary: This document specifies DHCPv6, an extensible way to configure nodes with network parameters, IPv6 addresses and prefixes. Parameters can be given statelessly or together with stateful assignment of addresses and prefixes. It is an Internet Standard and obsoletes RFC 8415.

plainLanguage.summary: DHCPv6 lets an IPv6 device request network settings, addresses, or delegated prefixes from a server. It also defines how clients renew assignments and how relay agents carry messages to servers on other links.

questions: what udp ports does dhcpv6 use
subtitle: Configures IPv6 nodes with addresses, delegated prefixes, and other network parameters.

tldr.problem: IPv6 nodes may need managed addresses, delegated prefixes, and settings such as DNS server information. Clients also need to renew assignments and communicate with servers that may be on another link.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv6 uses client/server messages over UDP, options for configuration and leases, and relay agents to carry messages between links.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9915 is the Internet Standard specification for DHCPv6. It obsoletes RFC 8415 and marks the IA_TA option, Server Unicast option, and UseMulticast status code obsolete.

today: RFC 9915 is Internet Standard STD 102, published in January 2026. It obsoletes RFC 8415.

sections.title: What DHCPv6 Provides
sections.content:
DHCPv6 is a client/server protocol for providing managed configuration to IPv6 nodes. A server can assign addresses, delegate prefixes, and return other configuration information through options.

A client can use stateless DHCPv6 to request configuration information without asking for an address or prefix. DHCPv6 can be used with or instead of stateless address autoconfiguration. This RFC obsoletes RFC 8415, applies verified errata, and removes several features that the RFC says were not widely implemented.
sections.plainLanguage: A client can ask DHCPv6 for settings, addresses, or network prefixes. The client can request settings alone or combine them with address or prefix assignment.

sections.title: Finding a Server and Getting a Lease
sections.content:
For address or prefix assignment, a client normally sends Solicit to locate servers. Servers can answer with Advertise; the client selects a server and sends Request; the selected server returns Reply with configuration and leases.

A client that needs only other settings sends Information-request and receives Reply. A client may request an expedited Solicit/Reply exchange with the Rapid Commit option, but a server may decline to use it. Clients later send Renew to extend lease lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first finds servers, then selects one and requests its configuration. A client that needs only settings can ask for them without requesting a lease.

sections.title: Message Headers and Relay Agents
sections.content:
Client and server messages share a fixed header with a one-octet message type and a three-octet transaction ID, followed by options. The transaction ID helps match a reply to its request. Options follow one another without padding.

Relay-forward and Relay-reply messages use a different header, including a hop count, link address, and peer address. A relay agent places the original DHCP message inside a Relay Message option so a server on another link can process it.
sections.plainLanguage: Each client/server message identifies its type and transaction, then carries options. A relay wraps the original message and forwards it between links.

sections.title: Client Identity, Leases, and Prefixes
sections.content:
Each client and server has a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID). A DUID begins with a two-octet type code and carries an identifier from one to 128 octets. Implementations treat DUIDs as opaque and compare them for equality.

An Identity Association groups related addresses or delegated prefixes. The client chooses an IAID for each association; it must remain consistent across client restarts. The T1 timer indicates when to ask the assigning server to renew, and T2 indicates when to ask any server to rebind.

A delegated prefix can be divided by the client for links in its own network. Addresses or prefixes derived from it must not outlive the delegated prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: A DUID identifies a DHCP participant, and an Identity Association groups the leases assigned to it. Renewal timers tell the client when to contact a server again.

sections.title: Retransmission and Rate Limits
sections.content:
Clients are responsible for reliable delivery of client-initiated exchanges. If a client does not receive the expected response, it retransmits using an increasing timeout with a random factor. The client updates the Elapsed Time option when it retransmits.

Clients must limit how quickly they send messages, with the limit enforced separately for each interface. The RFC recommends a token-bucket method and gives 20 messages in 20 seconds as a possible default. A random delay before the first Solicit can reduce synchronized requests after an outage.
sections.plainLanguage: If a server does not reply, the client waits longer between retransmissions. Clients also limit their message rate so repeated requests do not create a burst.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
DHCPv6 does not provide end-to-end encryption between clients and servers, so messages can be hijacked, changed, or observed. A malicious server could provide incorrect settings, and clients or servers can face resource-exhaustion attacks. IPsec can protect messages between relay agents and servers.

The Reconfiguration Key Authentication Protocol protects Reconfigure messages. A client must discard an unauthenticated Reconfigure message or one that fails validation. The RFC notes that an attacker who intercepts the initial exchange can obtain the key. It refers to separate RFCs for DHCPv6 privacy risks and mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 messages are not encrypted end to end, so clients need to consider who can send or observe them. Reconfigure messages require authentication, and client identifiers can raise privacy concerns.
